meta.blurb: A good man loses everything in a single day. Three friends sit beside him, and then the arguments begin. Read the ancient Book of Job, the great story of suffering, honest questions and a voice from the whirlwind.
meta.bible: Book of Job: a book of the Hebrew Bible, also part of the Christian Old Testament, a story in prose and poetry about a good man who suffers. Job: the man at the centre of the book, blameless and honest. Hebrew. Bible. Uz: the land where Job lived, whose exact place is not known. God. The Lord: the name that most English translations use for the name of God. Accuser. The accuser: in Hebrew ha-satan, a member of the heavenly court who tests Job, not yet the devil of later tradition. Satan. Sabeans and Chaldeans: raiders who attack Job's herds. Eliphaz: the first friend, from Teman. Bildad: the second friend, from Shuah. Zophar: the third friend, from Naamah. Teman. Shuah. Naamah. Elihu: a younger man who speaks late in the book. Behemoth and Leviathan: two huge creatures that God describes. Pleiades: a cluster of stars that God mentions. Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-Happuch: the names of Job's three new daughters. Ayyub: the name of Job in Islam, where he is remembered as a patient prophet. Islam. Quran. James: a letter of the New Testament that mentions the patience of Job. New Testament. Old Testament. Jews. Christians. Fixed facts: Job begins with seven sons and three daughters, seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred pairs of oxen and five hundred donkeys. He is covered with painful sores. His friends sit silently with him for seven days and nights. At the end he has twice as many animals, seven sons and three daughters again, and lives another one hundred and forty years. Voice and tone: calm, serious, warm and respectful. Every idea is attributed to the book. The words are retold, never long quotations. Where a verse can be translated in more than one way, say so. Never preach or compare faiths.

B1B2: The Book of Job is an ancient story and poem from the Hebrew Bible. It asks one of the hardest questions of all, which is why good people sometimes suffer.
Job lives in the land of Uz, and the book calls him blameless and honest, a man who respects God. He has seven sons and three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, and a very large household.
One day the heavenly beings come to stand before God, and the accuser comes with them. God asks whether he has noticed Job, who is blameless and honest and has no equal on earth.
The accuser answers that Job is only good because God has blessed him with so much. If everything were taken away, he says, Job would curse God, so God allows him to be tested.

Four messengers rush to Job on the same day, each one arriving before the last has finished speaking. Raiders have taken his oxen, donkeys and camels, fire has burned his sheep, and a great wind has killed all his children.

Job stands up, tears his robe and shaves his head, and then he falls to the ground in worship. He says that he came into the world with nothing and will leave it with nothing, and he blesses the name of the Lord.

In a second scene in heaven, the accuser claims that a person will give up anything to save his own skin. God allows him to harm Job's body, though not to take his life, and Job is soon covered with painful sores.
Job's wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers that people should accept bad things from God as well as good, and the book says that he did not sin with his lips.

Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, hear about Job's troubles and travel to comfort him. They hardly recognise him, and they sit on the ground with him for seven days and nights without saying a word.
At last Job breaks the silence, and he curses the day he was born. He wishes that the day had been dark and had never been counted among the days of the year.
Job asks why light is given to people in misery, and why life is given to those who are bitter. What he feared has come upon him, he says, and he finds no peace or quiet.
Eliphaz speaks gently at first, reminding Job that he once comforted others. Then he asks who that was innocent ever perished, and says that those who plant trouble will reap it.

Job answers that his friends are like desert streams, which flow in winter but vanish in the heat just when travellers need them. He adds that his life is only a breath, and his days pass faster than a weaver's shuttle.
Bildad, the second friend, insists that God never twists justice. He even suggests that Job's children died because they sinned, and he says that if Job is pure, God will restore him.
Job agrees that God is wise and powerful, so no person can win an argument with him. He longs for someone to stand between them, a referee who could put a hand on both and make things fair.
Zophar, the third friend, says that Job's words are empty and that God actually punishes him less than he deserves. He urges Job to put away his sin and he will find peace.
Job replies sarcastically that his friends are the only wise people, and that wisdom will die with them. He says that even the animals and the birds could teach them that God made all things.
Job says that human life is short and full of trouble, like a flower that withers. A tree that is cut down may sprout again from its stump, but a man who dies does not rise.
In the second round, Eliphaz says that wicked people suffer all their days. Job calls his friends miserable comforters, and he asks when their windy words will come to an end.
Job says that even now his witness is in heaven, and that the one who speaks for him is on high. While his friends laugh at him, his eyes pour out tears to God.
Bildad describes in dark pictures how the wicked come to a terrible end. Job answers that his brothers, friends and servants all keep away from him, and he begs them to have pity.
Job wishes that his words could be carved into rock for ever. He says that he knows his redeemer lives, and that he will see God in the end, although this passage is hard to translate.
Zophar says that the joy of the wicked lasts only a moment. Job answers that in real life the wicked often grow old, become powerful and see their children do well.

In the third round, Eliphaz suddenly accuses Job of cruel acts, such as refusing water to the thirsty and bread to the hungry. Nothing in the story says that Job did these things, and the narrator has already called him blameless.

Job says that if only he knew where to find God, he would go to his court and state his case. He goes east and west, north and south, but God stays hidden, yet he believes that he will come out of the test like gold.

Job points to the world's injustice: the poor are pushed off the road, and the hungry carry sheaves for others. He asks why God does not set a time of judgment, since the dying groan and no one hears.
Bildad speaks only a few lines, saying that no human can be pure before God. Job answers that as long as he has breath, he will not lie, and he will never admit to wrong that he has not done.
A beautiful poem asks where wisdom can be found. People dig deep mines for silver and gold, but wisdom cannot be bought, and only God knows where it lives.

Job remembers the old days, when God watched over him and people stood up to honour him at the city gate. He rescued the poor and the orphan, he says, and he was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.
Now Job is laughed at by young men whose fathers he would not have trusted with his dogs. He cries out to God for help, but he says that no answer comes.
In a long final oath, Job lists what he has not done: he has not cheated, been cruel, or turned away the poor. He ends by asking the Almighty to answer him.

A younger man named Elihu, who has waited quietly because of his age, finally speaks. He is angry with Job for declaring himself right before God, and with the three friends for failing to answer him.
Elihu argues that God is always fair and that suffering can be a warning or a lesson. He ends by describing a great storm, with thunder, lightning, snow and rain, as a sign of how great God is.

Suddenly, God answers Job out of a whirlwind, which breaks the long silence at last. He asks who this is that darkens his plans with words without knowledge, and he tells Job to stand up like a man and answer.

God asks where Job was when the foundations of the earth were laid, when the morning stars sang together. He describes the sea as a baby that he wrapped in clouds and gave a border that the waves cannot cross.

God asks Job whether he has ever commanded the morning to begin, or entered the storehouses of snow and hail. He asks whether Job can bind the Pleiades, send out lightning, or tell the rain where to fall.
God now turns to the wild animals of the earth and sky. He is the one who finds prey for the lions, feeds the young ravens when they cry, and watches the mountain goats give birth.
God describes the wild ox that will not serve people and the war horse that charges into battle without fear. The hawk and the eagle soar high above the earth, and Job has no part in their flight.
Job answers that he is small, and he puts his hand over his mouth. God speaks again and asks whether Job would condemn God to make himself look right, and whether he has an arm like God's.
God describes two mighty creatures, Behemoth and Leviathan, which no human can tame. Readers often think of a hippopotamus and a crocodile, though some see mythical sea monsters.
Job tells God that he knows God can do all things and that no purpose of his can be stopped. He says that he had heard of God before, but now his own eyes have seen him.
God turns to Eliphaz and says that he and his friends have not spoken rightly about him, as his servant Job has. They must offer sacrifices, and Job will pray for them.
After Job prays for his friends, God restores his fortunes. His brothers, sisters and old friends come to eat with him and comfort him, and each gives him a piece of silver and a gold ring.
God blesses the last part of Job's life even more than the first. Job now has fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand pairs of oxen and a thousand donkeys, twice as many as before.
Job has seven more sons and three more daughters. He names the daughters Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-Happuch, and the book says that no women in the land were as beautiful as they were.
After this, Job lives for another hundred and forty years. He sees four generations of his family, and he dies an old man, full of days.
The book never tells Job about the conversation in heaven, and God does not explain why Job suffered. Instead, God shows him a world so wide and wonderful that it is far beyond human understanding.

The English phrase the patience of Job comes from the New Testament letter of James. Yet in the book itself, Job complains and argues loudly, so many readers see him as a man who protests as well as endures.

Job appears in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and he is also remembered in Islam as the prophet Ayyub. The Quran praises him as a patient man who called on his Lord in his distress and was healed.
The Book of Job does not promise easy answers. It honours the sufferer who speaks honestly, and it suggests that the best comfort may be a friend who sits quietly and listens.
C1C2: The Book of Job, part of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, is an ancient work that combines a short story with a long poem. It wrestles with one of the hardest questions that human beings ask, which is why good people sometimes suffer terrible pain. Nobody knows who wrote it, and most scholars date it somewhere between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE.

In the land of Uz, whose exact location is not known, there lived a man named Job, whom the book describes as blameless and upright, someone who respected God and turned away from evil. He had seven sons and three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, hundreds of oxen and donkeys, and so many servants that he was counted the greatest man in the east. After each family feast he would offer sacrifices on behalf of his children, in case they had carelessly done wrong.

The story then moves to heaven, where the heavenly beings gather before God, and the one called the accuser, in Hebrew ha-satan, arrives among them after roaming the earth. God asks whether he has noticed Job, a man with no equal on earth, blameless, upright and respectful of God. The figure here is a member of the heavenly court, and not yet the devil of later tradition, a point that scholars often stress.

The accuser is not impressed, and he replies that Job has good reason to respect God, since God has built a fence around him and has blessed everything he does. Take it all away, he says, and Job will curse you to your face. God accepts the challenge and allows the accuser to touch everything that Job owns, but forbids him to harm Job himself.

On a single day, while Job's children are feasting together, four messengers come to him in turn, each arriving while the last is still speaking. The first reports that raiders have carried off the oxen and donkeys, the second that fire from the sky has burned up the sheep, and the third that other raiders have taken the camels. The fourth brings the worst news of all, that a great wind has struck the house where his sons and daughters were eating, and that all of them are dead.

In his grief Job does what mourners of his time did, for he stands up, tears his robe and shaves his head, and then he falls to the ground in worship. Naked I came from my mother's womb, he says, and naked I will return, and the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away. In all this, the book states, Job did not sin or blame God for doing wrong.

In a second scene in heaven, the accuser answers that a person will give up anything to save his own skin, and that if Job's body were touched, he would surely curse God. God allows him to attack Job's health, though not to take his life, and the accuser goes out and strikes Job with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head. Job leaves his house and sits in the ashes, where he scrapes himself with a piece of broken pottery.

Watching her husband scrape his sores among the ashes, Job's wife asks whether he is still holding on to his integrity, and she tells him to curse God and die. Job answers that she is talking like a foolish woman, and he asks whether we should accept the good from God and not the bad as well. Throughout this first part of the story, the book says, Job did not sin in anything that he said.

Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, hear of Job's troubles and agree to travel together to sympathise with him and comfort him. When they see him from a distance they hardly recognise him, and they weep aloud, tear their robes and throw dust on their heads. Then they sit on the ground beside him for seven days and seven nights, and none of them says a word, for they see that his suffering is very great.

At last Job breaks the long silence, and what comes out is a cry of pure pain, in which he curses the day he was born. May that day turn to darkness, he says, and may God not look for it from above, and may no light shine on it. The poem that follows is among the most intense passages in the Bible, and it is notable that Job never curses God himself, only the day of his birth.

Job goes on to ask why he did not die at birth, for then he would now be lying quietly, at rest with kings and counsellors, where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at peace. Why is light given to those in misery, he asks, and life to the bitter of soul who long for death and cannot find it? What he feared most has come upon him, he says, and he has no peace, no quiet and no rest.

Eliphaz, the eldest of the friends, speaks first and begins gently, reminding Job that he once strengthened many people who were weak and that his own faith ought now to sustain him. Then he states the belief that governs all three friends, that the innocent do not perish and that those who plough evil and sow trouble reap the same. He describes a spirit that passed before his face at night and asked whether a mortal can be more righteous than God, and he advises Job to appeal to the God who heals the wounds that he causes.

Job answers that his complaint is as heavy as the sand of the seas, and that his friends have let him down like streams in the desert, which run full in winter but vanish in the heat just when travellers have most need of them. He speaks of human life as hard service, of days that pass faster than a weaver's shuttle, and of a life that is only a breath. In a bitter echo of a more famous psalm, he asks what a human being is that God should watch him every morning and test him every moment.

Bildad, the second friend, speaks more sharply, asking how long Job will go on talking such wind, and insisting that God does not pervert justice nor twist what is right. Harshly, he suggests that Job's children may have died because of their own wrongdoing, and he urges Job to seek God and to be pure and upright, in which case God will certainly restore him. The advice sounds orthodox, and yet it cannot be right, as the reader already knows that Job is innocent.

Job replies that he knows well enough that God is wise in heart and mighty in strength, and that no mortal can win an argument with such a being, who could answer a thousand questions with one overwhelming reply. Even if he were innocent, he says, God could still crush him with a storm, and who could demand that God explain himself? What he longs for is an umpire, someone who could place a hand on each of them and make the contest fair, but there is none.

Zophar, the third friend and the most impatient, asks whether such a torrent of words should go unanswered and whether a talker is proved right merely by talking. He claims that God is actually punishing Job less than his guilt deserves, and he asks whether Job can fathom the mystery of God or reach the limits of the Almighty. If Job will only put away his sin, Zophar promises, his life will shine brighter than noon, and he will lie down in safety and be free from fear.

Job replies with sarcasm that no doubt his friends are the people of the earth, and that wisdom will die with them, but he too has a mind, and none of what they have said is new to him. Ask the animals, he says, and they will teach you, and ask the birds of the air, and they will tell you that the hand of God has made all these things. He then declares that he wants to argue his case before God himself, and he adds a line that translators render in different ways, that even if God should slay him, he will still hope in him.

Mortals, born of woman, are few of days and full of trouble, Job says, and they come up like a flower and wither, and flee like a shadow and do not last. There is hope for a tree, for if it is cut down it will sprout again, and the scent of water may make it bud like a young plant, whereas a human being dies and is laid low. Still, Job allows himself to imagine that God might hide him in the grave until his anger has passed, and then call him back.

In the second round of speeches, Eliphaz grows more severe, accusing Job of undermining reverence for God with his words and claiming that the wicked are in torment all their days. Job's reply is weary and scornful, for he has heard many such things before, and he calls the three of them miserable comforters and asks whether there is no end to windy words. If their places were exchanged, he says, he could talk as they do, but he would rather encourage them with his mouth than with empty speeches.

Even now, Job declares, his witness is in heaven and the one who vouches for him is on high, as though he hoped that God himself would take his side against the God who seems to be afflicting him. While his friends scoff at him, his eyes pour out tears to God, and he pleads that someone may argue for him with God as a person argues for a friend. The thought is a strange one, since it implies that Job's last hope is to appeal from God to God.

Bildad draws a series of dark pictures of the fate of the wicked, whose light is put out and whose memory perishes from the earth, and Job knows that he is meant to see himself in them. In reply he lists all that he has lost, for his brothers keep their distance, his friends have forgotten him, his servants no longer answer when he calls, and even small children make fun of him. Have pity on me, he begs his friends, for the hand of God has struck me, and why do you hound me as God does?

Job wishes that his words could be written in a book, or cut with an iron tool into the rock for ever, so that someone might read them long after he is gone. I know that my redeemer lives, he says, and that in the end he will stand upon the earth, and I shall see God for myself, although the Hebrew here is difficult and translators disagree about almost every phrase. Christian tradition has often heard in these words a hope of resurrection, while many scholars read them as a hope that God will declare Job innocent before he dies.

Zophar insists that the triumph of the wicked is short and that the joy of the godless lasts but a moment, though he does not explain why this should be so obvious to everyone. Job answers him with the plain facts of life, which are that the wicked often live on, grow old and grow powerful, see their children established, and go down to their graves in peace. How often is the lamp of the wicked put out, he asks, and the answer that his friends cannot easily face is that it is not often.

In the third round of speeches, Eliphaz abandons all caution and accuses Job of specific crimes, saying that he gave no water to the weary, withheld bread from the hungry and sent widows away empty-handed. Nothing in the story suggests that Job did any of these things, and the narrator has already described him as blameless, so the reader sees that Eliphaz is inventing evidence to fit his theory. Even so, he ends with a gracious appeal that Job should submit to God and be at peace.

If only I knew where to find him, Job cries, I would go to his dwelling and lay out my case, and I would find that he listens to me instead of overpowering me. But he looks to the east and God is not there, he turns to the west and cannot see him, and he searches north and south without catching a glimpse. Yet he knows the way that I take, Job says, and when he has tested me, I will come forth like gold, a line that is often quoted as a sign of Job's persistent trust.

Job turns from his own case to the injustice of the world at large, where the wicked move boundary stones, steal the donkey of the orphan, push the needy off the road and leave the poor to hide. The poor go about naked and hungry and carry sheaves for others, he says, and the groans of the dying rise from the city, but God seems to pay no attention to their prayers. Why does the Almighty not set times of judgment, he asks, and why do those who know him never see his days of justice?

Bildad's third speech is only a few lines long, and it can only repeat that no human being can be righteous before God, who makes the moon itself seem dim and the stars unclean. Job answers with irony, asking what help Bildad has offered to the powerless, and he speaks about the immense power of God, of whom we hear only a whisper. As long as I have life in me, he swears, my lips will speak no wrong, and until I die I will not give up my integrity.

At this point a quiet poem interrupts the arguments, and it begins by describing how human beings dig deep mines for silver, gold, iron and precious stones, sinking shafts into the darkness far from where anyone lives. But where, it asks, can wisdom be found, for it cannot be bought with gold or silver, and the sea and the deep say that it is not with them. Only God understands the way to it, and to human beings he has said that to respect the Lord is wisdom and to turn from evil is understanding.

Job now turns to the past, and he remembers the months when God watched over him, when the young men stepped aside and the old rose to their feet as he came to the city gate. He had rescued the poor who cried for help and the orphan with no one to help, he says, and he had put on righteousness as if it were a robe. I was eyes to the blind, he recalls, and feet to the lame, and I was a father to the needy.

Now, by contrast, Job is mocked by young men whose fathers he would not even have trusted with the dogs of his flock, and they spit in his face and do not hide their scorn. His dignity has been blown away like smoke, he says, and his days of suffering have taken hold of him, so that his bones burn with fever and his skin turns dark. I cry out to you, God, he says, and you do not answer, and I stand up, but you merely look at me.

In his last great speech Job swears an oath of innocence, stating that he has made a covenant with his eyes, that he has not walked with falsehood, and that he has not been unfair to his servants. He has not put his trust in gold, he says, nor been glad when his enemy was ruined, and he has opened his door to the traveller. Let the Almighty answer me, he finishes, and if my accuser has written out his charge, I would wear it proudly like a crown. With that, the words of Job are ended.

A new speaker, Elihu, a younger man who has waited in silence because the others were older, can no longer hold his tongue, and he is angry both with Job for justifying himself and with the three friends for condemning Job without proving him wrong. It is not only the old who are wise, he says, and it is the spirit within a person that gives understanding. He claims that God does speak to people, in dreams and in the pain of the sickbed, to turn them from a wrong path and to save them from the pit.

Over several chapters, Elihu insists that God cannot do wrong and that the Almighty does not pervert justice, and that suffering may serve as a warning or a school for those whom God wishes to teach. His final speech is a hymn to the greatness of God in the weather, which describes thunder, lightning, snow, rain and the cold that comes from the north, and it grows louder as a real storm seems to gather. Elihu receives no answer in the book, and some scholars think that his speeches were added later, although the story as we have it includes them.

Then, out of the whirlwind, the Lord himself answers Job, at last breaking the long silence that Job has complained of from the beginning. Who is this, he asks, that darkens counsel with words that lack knowledge, and he tells Job to brace himself like a man, for he will question Job and Job must answer. What follows is not an explanation of Job's suffering, but a tour of the wonders of the world, set before him as a series of questions.

Where were you, God asks, when I laid the foundations of the earth, when the morning stars sang together and all the heavenly beings shouted for joy, and who set its measurements and stretched the measuring line across it? He then describes the birth of the sea as a baby bursting from the womb, wrapped in clouds as in swaddling clothes, and held back by doors and bars. Thus far you may come, he says to its waves, and no farther, and here your proud waves must stop.

God goes on to ask whether Job has ever commanded the morning or shown the dawn its place so that it might take the earth by its edges and shake the wicked out of it. He asks whether Job has entered the storehouses of the snow, whether he can bind the cluster of the Pleiades or loosen the belt of Orion, and whether he can send out lightning bolts that report to him. Who, he asks, has cut a channel for the torrents of rain, and who has fathered the dew, the ice and the frost?

Then God turns from the sky to the wild animals, and he asks whether Job hunts the prey for the lioness and satisfies the hunger of the young lions as they crouch in their dens. Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God, he asks, and do you know when the mountain goats give birth, or watch the deer as they bear their fawns? The wild donkey, which scorns the noise of the city and roams the hills as its pasture, runs free without any master.

God continues with the wild ox that will not be tied to a plough, and then, with evident admiration, with the war horse, whose neck is clothed with a mane and who laughs at fear as it charges into battle. The hawk, he says, soars by no wisdom of Job's, and the eagle does not build its nest on the heights at Job's command. From its home among the cliffs the eagle spies out its food, and its keen eyes see it from far away.

Job's first answer is brief, for he says that he is of small account and cannot reply, and that he will put his hand over his mouth and speak no more. God, however, answers again from the whirlwind and asks whether Job will really condemn him in order to justify himself, and whether he has an arm like God's and a voice that thunders as his does. He invites Job to put on glory and splendour, to look on the proud and humble them, and says that then he himself will admit that Job's own right hand can save him.

At the end of his speeches, God describes two huge creatures: Behemoth, which feeds on grass like an ox but has bones like bronze, and Leviathan, a monster of the water whose scales are like rows of shields. Many readers have taken them to be the hippopotamus and the crocodile, whereas others think that they are mythical beasts of chaos, which God alone can command. In either case, the point is that Job cannot catch or tame them, and that the world contains forces much larger than he can control.

Job's last reply is short and moving, for he tells God that he knows he can do all things and that no purpose of his can be thwarted, and that he spoke of things that he did not understand. I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, he says, but now my eye sees you, and therefore I retract, and I repent in dust and ashes. The last phrase can be translated in different ways, and while some readers hear repentance for sin, others hear Job taking comfort, now that he is a mortal in the presence of God.

After speaking to Job, God turns to Eliphaz and says that his anger burns against him and his two friends, because they have not spoken of him what is right, as his servant Job has. Remarkably, the one who complained so loudly is honoured, and the ones who defended God with careful theology are rebuked, and they are told to bring seven bulls and seven rams for a sacrifice. Job will pray for them, God says, and he will accept the prayer of Job, which brings the three friends and the sufferer together again.

When Job prays for his friends, the Lord restores his fortunes, and the family and friends who had stayed away during his suffering now come to his house and eat bread with him. They show him sympathy and comfort him over all the trouble that the Lord had brought on him, and each one gives him a piece of silver and a gold ring. The comfort comes late, but it comes, and it suggests that the ordinary kindness of other people is part of how a sufferer heals.

The Lord blesses the latter part of Job's life even more than the first, and the book gives the exact count of his new wealth. He now has fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen and a thousand donkeys, each a double of what he lost at the beginning. Readers have long noted that the double portion cannot undo the loss of the ten children, and that restoration, in the book, is a gift and not a payment.

Job is blessed with seven new sons and three new daughters, and, unusually, the book names only the daughters, calling them Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-Happuch. No women in all the land, it says, were as beautiful as the daughters of Job, and their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers. In the ancient world this was a surprising thing to do, and it shows that Job has learned a new kind of generosity.

After all these events, Job lives another hundred and forty years, long enough to see his children, his grandchildren, and his great-grandchildren growing up around him. The book ends calmly, with the statement that he died old and full of days, as though the storm of the story had finally passed. The ending is quiet, and the reader is left with the sense of a life that was broken and mended.

Strangely, Job is never told about the scenes in heaven, and God never explains why he suffered, or says that the suffering was a punishment, or says that it was a test that he has now passed. Instead he is shown a world of such size and wonder, and so full of wild creatures that humans do not control, that his own question seems small beside it. Scholars still disagree about whether this is a comfort, a rebuke or something more, and the book leaves it open.

The English phrase the patience of Job comes from the letter of James in the New Testament, which holds up Job as an example of endurance in trouble. Yet in the book itself, Job is anything but quiet, for he complains, accuses and argues with God at length, so that many readers see in him a man of protest as much as a man of patience. Both pictures capture something, and the book itself seems to value his honest struggle above any easy calm.

Job belongs to the Writings of the Hebrew Bible and to the Old Testament of Christians, and he is also remembered in Islam, where he is known as Ayyub, one of the prophets. The Quran, which is much shorter on the subject, speaks of him as a patient man who called out to his Lord in his affliction and was healed, and whose family was restored to him. The story of a person who suffers greatly and does not lose hold of God has thus been told, in different forms, by several of the world's faiths.

The Book of Job offers no easy answers, and perhaps that is why it has been read for more than two thousand years by people in pain and by those who love them. It honours the sufferer who speaks honestly, it distrusts the friend who explains too quickly, and it hints that the kindest thing may be what the three friends did at first, which was to sit down beside the sufferer and say nothing. Whatever readers conclude about God, they find in Job a companion who asks the hardest questions without turning away.
